items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide, producing a torque but no resultant force"?
items.answer: couple
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of couple.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a couple and a torque.
items.answer: A torque is the turning effect of any force about an axis; a couple is a specific pair of equal and opposite forces that produces a pure torque with no resultant force.
items.markingKey: A torque is the turning effect of any force about an axis; a couple is a specific pair of equal and opposite forces that produces a pure torque with no resultant force. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the position of the axis does not matter when taking moments for a body in equilibrium.
items.answer: If the resultant force is zero and the resultant torque is zero about one point, it is zero about every point, so any convenient point (often through an unknown force) can be chosen.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If the resultant force is zero and the resultant torque is zero about one point, it is zero about every point, so any convenient point (often through an unknown force) can be chosen. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A uniform beam of length 3.0 m and weight 100 N rests horizontally on supports at its ends. A 200 N load is placed 1.0 m from the left end. Calculate the force exerted by the right-hand support.
items.markingKey: Moments about the left support: R × 3.0 = 100 × 1.5 + 200 × 1.0 (M1); R = 117 N (A1).

items.stem: Kenji applies a force of 120 N to a wheel brace of length 0.25 m at 45° to the handle. Calculate the torque about the nut.
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Cranes can lift any load as long as their counterweight is heavy enough."
items.answer: Counterweights extend capacity, but structural strength, stability when unloaded and wind limit the safe load.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a larger counterweight balances a larger load moment. Arguments against: the structure, cable and foundations have limited strength; an unloaded crane with a huge counterweight could topple backwards; wind loads add torque. Supported judgement: Counterweights extend capacity, but structural strength, stability when unloaded and wind limit the safe load.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "centre of mass"?
options: The point at which the whole mass of a body may be considered to be concentrated
The rotational analogue of linear momentum, L = Iω, in kg m² s⁻¹
A pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide, producing a torque but no resultant force
The state in which the resultant torque on a body about any axis is zero
items.answer: The point at which the whole mass of a body may be considered to be concentrated
items.markingKey: A. "centre of mass" is the point at which the whole mass of a body may be considered to be concentrated.

items.stem: A uniform metre rule balances at its 50 cm mark. A 0.20 N weight is hung at the 10 cm mark. Where must a 0.40 N weight be hung to restore balance?
items.answer: At the 70 cm mark

items.stem: Elena is revising torque, moments and rotational equilibrium. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A larger torque always produces a larger angular velocity.
If angular momentum is conserved, rotational kinetic energy must also be conserved.
A spinning object needs a continuous torque to keep spinning.
Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ).
items.answer: Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ).
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ).

items.stem: "Torque depends only on the size of the force." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ).
items.markingKey: Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.3 m by applying equal and opposite tangential forces of 5.0 N with each hand at opposite ends of a diameter. Calculate the torque of the couple.
items.markingKey: Torque of couple = F × separation (M1) = 5.0 × 0.3 = 1.50 N m (A1).

items.stem: A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.2 m by applying equal and opposite tangential forces of 8.0 N with each hand at opposite ends of a diameter. Calculate the torque of the couple.
items.markingKey: C. Torque of couple = F × separation (M1) = 8.0 × 0.2 = 1.60 N m (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Torque depends only on the size of the force." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ).
items.markingKey: Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
This question is about torque, moments and rotational equilibrium.

(a) On a seesaw in a park in Toronto, a 35 kg child sits 1.0 m from the pivot. Calculate the distance from the pivot on the other side at which a 60 kg child must sit to balance it. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain why a long-handled wrench makes it easier to undo a tight nut. [3]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Cranes can lift any load as long as their counterweight is heavy enough." [4]
items.answer: (a) 0.583 m (b) Torque = force × perpendicular distance; a longer handle increases the distance, so the required torque is achieved with a smaller force. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) Counterweights extend capacity, but structural strength, stability when unloaded and wind limit the safe load.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Principle of moments: 35g × 1.0 = 60g × d (M1); d = 0.583 m (A1). (b) [3 marks] Torque = force × perpendicular distance; a longer handle increases the distance, so the required torque is achieved with a smaller force. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [4 marks] For: a larger counterweight balances a larger load moment. Against: the structure, cable and foundations have limited strength; an unloaded crane with a huge counterweight could topple backwards; wind loads add torque. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Counterweights extend capacity, but structural strength, stability when unloaded and wind limit the safe load.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "angular displacement"?
options: The product of torque and the time for which it acts, τΔt, equal to the change in angular momentum
The angle in radians through which a body rotates about an axis
A pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide, producing a torque but no resultant force
The linear speed of a point on a rotating body, v = ωr
items.answer: The angle in radians through which a body rotates about an axis
items.markingKey: B. "angular displacement" is the angle in radians through which a body rotates about an axis.

items.stem: A wheel’s angular velocity changes from 10 rad s⁻¹ to 30 rad s⁻¹ in 4.0 s. The angular displacement in this time is
items.answer: 80 rad

items.stem: A student claims: "The suvat equations for rotation work with any angular acceleration." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Like linear suvat, the rotational equations require constant angular acceleration.
items.markingKey: Like linear suvat, the rotational equations require constant angular acceleration. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A grindstone has an angular acceleration of 1.5 rad s⁻². Calculate the tangential acceleration of a point on its rim, 0.1 m from the axis.
Tomás rides a bicycle at 12 m s⁻¹ in Melbourne. The wheels have radius 0.4 m and roll without slipping. Calculate the angular velocity of the wheels.
items.answer: 30.0 rad s⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. ω = v/r (M1) = 30.0 rad s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A wind turbine’s blades, 40 m long, accelerate uniformly from rest to 18 revolutions per minute in 60 s, then rotate steadily. (a) Calculate the final angular velocity. (b) Calculate the angular acceleration. (c) Determine the number of revolutions made while accelerating. (d) Calculate the tip speed at full speed and suggest why tip speed is limited in design.
items.answer: (a) ω = 18 × 2π/60 = 1.88 rad s⁻¹; (b) α = 0.0314 rad s⁻²; (c) θ = ½ × 1.88 × 60 = 56.5 rad = 9.0 rev; (d) v = ωr = 75.4 m s⁻¹; high tip speeds cause noise, erosion of blade edges and large stresses.
items.markingKey: (a) ω = 18 × 2π/60 = 1.88 rad s⁻¹; (b) α = 0.0314 rad s⁻²; (c) θ = ½ × 1.88 × 60 = 56.5 rad = 9.0 rev; (d) v = ωr = 75.4 m s⁻¹; high tip speeds cause noise, erosion of blade edges and large stresses.

items.stem: Which equation is the rotational analogue of v² = u² + 2as?
items.answer: ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ
items.markingKey: B. Replace s, u, v, a with θ, ω₀, ω, α.

items.stem: Amara is revising angular displacement, velocity and acceleration; equations of rotational motion. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Like linear suvat, the rotational equations require constant angular acceleration.
A body can only have angular momentum if it spins about its own axis.
A spinning object needs a continuous torque to keep spinning.
The centre of mass of an object must lie within the material of the object.
items.answer: Like linear suvat, the rotational equations require constant angular acceleration.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. Like linear suvat, the rotational equations require constant angular acceleration.

items.stem: Explain how the area under an angular velocity–time graph is interpreted.
items.answer: Area = ω × t = angular displacement θ, analogous to displacement from a v–t graph.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Area = ω × t = angular displacement θ, analogous to displacement from a v–t graph. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between tangential velocity and angular velocity.
items.answer: Angular velocity (rad s⁻¹) is the rate of rotation and is the same for every point of a rigid body; tangential velocity (m s⁻¹) is the linear speed of a particular point, v = ωr, which increases with distance from the axis.
items.markingKey: Angular velocity (rad s⁻¹) is the rate of rotation and is the same for every point of a rigid body; tangential velocity (m s⁻¹) is the linear speed of a particular point, v = ωr, which increases with distance from the axis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mei writes: "Angular acceleration has units of rad s⁻¹." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, so its unit is rad s⁻².
items.markingKey: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, so its unit is rad s⁻². 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A drill bit accelerates uniformly from rest to 1800 rpm in 4.0 s. Calculate its angular acceleration.
items.answer: 47.1 rad s⁻²

items.stem:
This question is about angular displacement, velocity and acceleration; equations of rotational motion.

(a) A turntable rotating at 5.0 rad s⁻¹ has a constant angular acceleration of 3.0 rad s⁻². Calculate its angular velocity after it has turned through a further 20 rad. [2]

(b) Explain the difference between tangential velocity and angular velocity. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Using revolutions per minute is just as good as radians per second for physics calculations." [4]
items.answer: (a) 12.0 rad s⁻¹ (b) Angular velocity (rad s⁻¹) is the rate of rotation and is the same for every point of a rigid body; tangential velocity (m s⁻¹) is the linear speed of a particular point, v = ωr, which increases with distance from the axis. (c) rpm is convenient for communication but must be converted to rad s⁻¹ for calculations because the core equations rely on radian measure.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ (M1); ω = 12.0 rad s⁻¹ (A1). (b) [4 marks] Angular velocity (rad s⁻¹) is the rate of rotation and is the same for every point of a rigid body; tangential velocity (m s⁻¹) is the linear speed of a particular point, v = ωr, which increases with distance from the axis. (c) [4 marks] For: rpm is intuitive and used by engineers and on dashboards. Against: v = ωr, a = ω²r and τ = Iα only hold with radians; conversion errors are common. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: rpm is convenient for communication but must be converted to rad s⁻¹ for calculations because the core equations rely on radian measure.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rotational inertia"?
options: The rotational analogue of mass, I = Σmr², which measures a body’s resistance to angular acceleration about an axis
The property of a body that resists changes to its angular velocity, quantified by I
The angle in radians through which a body rotates about an axis
The rotational analogue of linear momentum, L = Iω, in kg m² s⁻¹
items.answer: The property of a body that resists changes to its angular velocity, quantified by I
items.markingKey: B. "rotational inertia" is the property of a body that resists changes to its angular velocity, quantified by I.

items.stem: Explain why the moment of inertia of an object depends on the axis of rotation.
items.answer: I = Σmr² depends on how far each mass element is from the axis; changing the axis changes the distances.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: I = Σmr² depends on how far each mass element is from the axis; changing the axis changes the distances. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Two objects with the same mass must have the same moment of inertia." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: I depends on the distribution of mass relative to the axis, so objects of equal mass can have very different I.
items.markingKey: I depends on the distribution of mass relative to the axis, so objects of equal mass can have very different I. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A solid disc rolls without slipping from rest down a slope of vertical height 1.5 m. Using I = 0.5MR², calculate its speed at the bottom.

A flywheel is mounted on an axle of radius 0.020 m. A cord wound on the axle supports a hanging mass m. The angular acceleration α is measured with a rotary sensor. For small masses the torque is approximately mgr. Theory: mgr = Iα.

m / kg | α / rad s⁻²
0.050 | 0.209
0.100 | 0.423
0.150 | 0.632
0.200 | 0.859
0.250 | 1.060
0.300 | 1.267

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the moment of inertia I of the flywheel. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State I with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) α (y) against torque mgr (x); (b) gradient ≈ 21.6 kg⁻¹ m⁻²; (c) 0.0462 kg m²; (d) 0.0462 kg m² ± 9 × 10⁻⁴ kg m²
items.markingKey: (a) α (y) against torque mgr (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 21.6 kg⁻¹ m⁻² – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) I = 1/gradient = 0.0462 kg m² (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 9 × 10⁻⁴ kg m²; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: Two small masses of 1.0 kg each are fixed to a light rod at distances 0.1 m and 0.3 m from the axis of rotation. Calculate the moment of inertia of the system.
items.answer: 0.100 kg m²

items.stem: A 1.5 kg bucket hangs from a rope wound around a solid cylindrical drum (mass 4.0 kg, radius 0.1 m, I = ½MR²) on a frictionless axle over a well. The system is released from rest. (a) Write equations for the linear motion of the hanging mass and the rotation of the drum. (b) Determine the acceleration of the hanging mass. (c) Calculate the tension in the rope. (d) Calculate the angular velocity of the drum after the mass has fallen 1.0 m and verify the result using energy conservation.
items.answer: (b) 4.20 m s⁻²; (c) 8.41 N; (d) v = 2.90 m s⁻¹, ω = 29.0 rad s⁻¹; energy: mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² gives the same v.
items.markingKey: (a) mg − T = ma; TR = Iα with α = a/R (M1 M1). (b) a = mg/(m + M/2) (A1). (c) T = ½Ma (A1). (d) v² = 2ah, ω = v/R (A1); energy check (R1).

items.stem: "Flywheels are a practical alternative to batteries for storing energy." Discuss.
items.answer: Flywheels are excellent for short-term, high-power storage (grid frequency control, buses, F1 KERS), but batteries are better for long-duration storage.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: high power output and rapid charging; long lifetime with many cycles; no toxic chemicals. Arguments against: energy leaks away by friction (self-discharge); large stresses in fast-spinning rotors – safety containment needed; lower energy per unit mass than batteries. Supported judgement: Flywheels are excellent for short-term, high-power storage (grid frequency control, buses, F1 KERS), but batteries are better for long-duration storage. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The rotational analogue of mass, I = Σmr², which measures a body’s resistance to angular acceleration about an axis"?
items.answer: moment of inertia
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of moment of inertia.

items.stem: Which has the larger moment of inertia about its central axis: a ring or a disc of the same mass and radius?
items.answer: The ring
items.markingKey: C. All the ring’s mass is at r; I_ring = MR², I_disc = ½MR².

items.stem: A figure skater pulls her arms in while spinning. Her moment of inertia
items.answer: decreases
items.markingKey: B. Mass moves closer to the axis.

items.stem: Distinguish between moment of inertia and mass.
items.answer: Mass measures resistance to linear acceleration and is fixed; moment of inertia measures resistance to angular acceleration and depends on how mass is distributed about the chosen axis.
items.markingKey: Mass measures resistance to linear acceleration and is fixed; moment of inertia measures resistance to angular acceleration and depends on how mass is distributed about the chosen axis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Alessia writes: "The moment of inertia of a rod is the same about any axis." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A rod of length L has I = ML²/12 about its centre but ML²/3 about one end.
items.markingKey: A rod of length L has I = ML²/12 about its centre but ML²/3 about one end. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Calculate the moment of inertia of a thin spherical shell of mass 10 kg and radius 0.1 m about its central axis (I = (2/3)MR²).
items.answer: 0.0667 kg m²

items.stem: Two small masses of 0.2 kg each are fixed to a light rod at distances 0.1 m and 0.5 m from the axis of rotation. Calculate the moment of inertia of the system.
items.answer: 0.0520 kg m²

items.stem:
This question is about moment of inertia and Newton's second law for rotation.

(a) A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a slope of vertical height 2.0 m. Using I = 0.4MR², calculate its speed at the bottom. [3]

(b) Explain why a solid cylinder rolls down a slope faster than a hoop of the same mass and radius. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Flywheels are a practical alternative to batteries for storing energy." [4]
items.answer: (a) 5.29 m s⁻¹ (b) Both convert the same GPE to KE; the hoop has a larger I, so a bigger fraction of the energy goes into rotation and less into translation, giving a lower speed. (c) Flywheels are excellent for short-term, high-power storage (grid frequency control, buses, F1 KERS), but batteries are better for long-duration storage.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² = ½mv²(1 + 0.4) (M1); v = √(2gh/(1 + 0.4)) = 5.29 m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) [3 marks] Both convert the same GPE to KE; the hoop has a larger I, so a bigger fraction of the energy goes into rotation and less into translation, giving a lower speed. (c) [4 marks] For: high power output and rapid charging; long lifetime with many cycles; no toxic chemicals. Against: energy leaks away by friction (self-discharge); large stresses in fast-spinning rotors – safety containment needed; lower energy per unit mass than batteries. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Flywheels are excellent for short-term, high-power storage (grid frequency control, buses, F1 KERS), but batteries are better for long-duration storage.

items.stem: A 2.0 kg bucket hangs from a rope wound around a solid cylindrical drum of mass 8.0 kg and radius 0.15 m (I = ½MR²) mounted on a frictionless axle. The bucket is released. (a) Write Newton’s second law for the bucket and for the drum. (b) Show that a = mg/(m + M/2) and calculate it. (c) Calculate the tension in the rope. (d) Determine the angular velocity of the drum after the bucket has fallen 2.0 m.
Which term matches this description: "The product of torque and the time for which it acts, τΔt, equal to the change in angular momentum"?
items.answer: angular impulse
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of angular impulse.

items.stem: Explain the difference between angular momentum and linear momentum.
items.answer: Linear momentum p = mv is conserved when no external force acts; angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when no external torque acts. Both are vectors.
items.markingKey: Linear momentum p = mv is conserved when no external force acts; angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when no external torque acts. Both are vectors. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: If the angular velocity of a flywheel doubles, its rotational kinetic energy
items.answer: quadruples
items.markingKey: A. E ∝ ω².

items.stem: Mei writes: "If angular momentum is conserved, rotational kinetic energy must also be conserved." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: E = L²/2I: when I changes at constant L, the kinetic energy changes; e.g. a skater increases her KE by doing work pulling her arms in.
items.markingKey: E = L²/2I: when I changes at constant L, the kinetic energy changes; e.g. a skater increases her KE by doing work pulling her arms in. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A rotor with moment of inertia 1.5 kg m² spins at 20 rad s⁻¹. Calculate its angular momentum.
items.answer: 30.0 kg m² s⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. L = Iω (M1) = 30.0 kg m² s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A playground roundabout (a disc of mass 120 kg, radius 1.5 m, I = ½MR²) rotates at 1.2 rad s⁻¹. A 40 kg child steps on at the rim from rest (relative to the ground). (a) Calculate the initial angular momentum. (b) Determine the new angular velocity. (c) Calculate the change in rotational kinetic energy and explain where the energy goes. (d) The child walks to the centre; determine the angular velocity then.
items.answer: (a) I = 135 kg m², L = 162 kg m² s⁻¹; (b) I = 135 + 90 = 225, ω = 0.72 rad s⁻¹; (c) 97.2 J → 58.3 J, 38.9 J lost to internal energy by friction as the child is brought up to speed; (d) back to 1.2 rad s⁻¹.
items.markingKey: (a) I = 135 kg m², L = 162 kg m² s⁻¹; (b) I = 135 + 90 = 225, ω = 0.72 rad s⁻¹; (c) 97.2 J → 58.3 J, 38.9 J lost to internal energy by friction as the child is brought up to speed; (d) back to 1.2 rad s⁻¹.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "angular momentum"?
options: The rate of change of angular displacement, ω = Δθ/Δt, in rad s⁻¹
The angle in radians through which a body rotates about an axis
The rotational analogue of linear momentum, L = Iω, in kg m² s⁻¹
The property of a body that resists changes to its angular velocity, quantified by I
items.answer: The rotational analogue of linear momentum, L = Iω, in kg m² s⁻¹
items.markingKey: C. "angular momentum" is the rotational analogue of linear momentum, L = Iω, in kg m² s⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why a helicopter needs a tail rotor.
items.answer: The engine exerts a torque on the main rotor; by Newton’s third law the rotor exerts an equal opposite torque on the body. Without the tail rotor’s counter-torque the body would spin to conserve angular momentum.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The engine exerts a torque on the main rotor; by Newton’s third law the rotor exerts an equal opposite torque on the body. Without the tail rotor’s counter-torque the body would spin to conserve angular momentum. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A teacher in Melbourne asks a class to choose the one correct statement about angular momentum, conservation and rotational kinetic energy. Which statement should be chosen?
options: Torque depends only on the size of the force.
The moment of inertia of a rod is the same about any axis.
A torque is only needed to change the angular velocity; with no resultant torque it spins at constant ω.
The centre of mass of an object must lie within the material of the object.
items.answer: A torque is only needed to change the angular velocity; with no resultant torque it spins at constant ω.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. A torque is only needed to change the angular velocity; with no resultant torque it spins at constant ω.

items.stem: A spinning wheel (I = 2.0 kg m²) at 20 rad s⁻¹ is stopped by a brake in 5.0 s. Calculate the average braking torque.
items.markingKey: τ = ΔL/Δt = Iω/t (M1) = 8.00 N m (A1).

items.answer: 0.565 rad s⁻¹

items.stem: "A spinning object needs a continuous torque to keep spinning." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A torque is only needed to change the angular velocity; with no resultant torque it spins at constant ω.
items.markingKey: A torque is only needed to change the angular velocity; with no resultant torque it spins at constant ω. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
This question is about angular momentum, conservation and rotational kinetic energy.

(a) A flywheel of moment of inertia 2.0 kg m² rotates at 300 rad s⁻¹. Calculate its rotational kinetic energy. [2]

(b) Explain why a diver tucks into a ball to perform somersaults. [3]

(c) "Conservation of angular momentum explains everything about how a cat lands on its feet." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of angular momentum, conservation and rotational kinetic energy. [4]
items.answer: (a) 9.00 × 10⁴ J (b) Once in the air no external torque acts (about the centre of mass), so L = Iω is constant; tucking reduces I, increasing ω so more rotations can be completed before entry. (c) Angular momentum conservation constrains the motion, but the cat’s trick is to rotate front and back halves by different amounts with zero total L; a single rigid-body model is insufficient.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] E = ½Iω² (M1) = 9.00 × 10⁴ J (A1). (b) [3 marks] Once in the air no external torque acts (about the centre of mass), so L = Iω is constant; tucking reduces I, increasing ω so more rotations can be completed before entry. (c) [4 marks] For: the cat changes its moment of inertia by tucking and extending legs. Against: the total angular momentum is zero throughout – the cat rotates parts of its body in opposite directions; a simple Iω = constant model cannot explain a turn from zero L; flexibility and reflexes matter. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Angular momentum conservation constrains the motion, but the cat’s trick is to rotate front and back halves by different amounts with zero total L; a single rigid-body model is insufficient.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about angular momentum, conservation and rotational kinetic energy is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Hana.)
options: If angular momentum is conserved, rotational kinetic energy must also be conserved.
I depends on the distribution of mass relative to the axis, so objects of equal mass can have very different I.
Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, so its unit is rad s⁻².
A rod of length L has I = ML²/12 about its centre but ML²/3 about one end.
items.answer: If angular momentum is conserved, rotational kinetic energy must also be conserved.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: E = L²/2I: when I changes at constant L, the kinetic energy changes; e.g. a skater increases her KE by doing work pulling her arms in.

items.stem: Ingrid is revising moment of inertia and Newton's second law for rotation. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A wheel rotating at constant angular velocity has no acceleration anywhere.
The moment of inertia of a rod is the same about any axis.
The suvat equations for rotation work with any angular acceleration.
Torque produces angular acceleration (τ = Iα); the angular velocity also depends on how long the torque acts and on the initial ω.
items.answer: Torque produces angular acceleration (τ = Iα); the angular velocity also depends on how long the torque acts and on the initial ω.
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Torque produces angular acceleration (τ = Iα); the angular velocity also depends on how long the torque acts and on the initial ω.

items.stem: A student in Cape Town is checking notes on torque, moments and rotational equilibrium. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ).
A torque is only needed to change the angular velocity; with no resultant torque it spins at constant ω.
Torque produces angular acceleration (τ = Iα); the angular velocity also depends on how long the torque acts and on the initial ω.
A body in equilibrium must have no forces acting on it.
items.answer: A body in equilibrium must have no forces acting on it.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Forces can act; equilibrium requires the resultant force and resultant torque to be zero.

items.stem: Isabel writes four statements while revising angular displacement, velocity and acceleration; equations of rotational motion. Which one is a misconception?
options: A rod of length L has I = ML²/12 about its centre but ML²/3 about one end.
Torque produces angular acceleration (τ = Iα); the angular velocity also depends on how long the torque acts and on the initial ω.
Torque also depends on the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action (τ = Fr sin θ).
A wheel rotating at constant angular velocity has no acceleration anywhere.
items.answer: A wheel rotating at constant angular velocity has no acceleration anywhere.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Angular acceleration is zero, but every point except the axis has centripetal acceleration ω²r towards the axis.

items.stem: Explain the difference between linear momentum and angular momentum.
items.answer: Linear momentum p = mv is conserved when no external force acts; angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when no external torque acts. Both are vectors.
items.markingKey: Linear momentum p = mv is conserved when no external force acts; angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when no external torque acts. Both are vectors. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between mass and moment of inertia.
items.answer: Mass measures resistance to linear acceleration and is fixed; moment of inertia measures resistance to angular acceleration and depends on how mass is distributed about the chosen axis.
items.markingKey: Mass measures resistance to linear acceleration and is fixed; moment of inertia measures resistance to angular acceleration and depends on how mass is distributed about the chosen axis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: It can lie outside, for example the centre of mass of a ring or a boomerang is in empty space.

items.stem:
This question is about moment of inertia and Newton's second law for rotation.

(a) Calculate the moment of inertia of a solid disc of mass 1.2 kg and radius 0.1 m about its central axis (I = ½MR²). [1]

(b) Explain why a solid cylinder rolls down a slope faster than a hoop of the same mass and radius. [3]

(c) "Flywheels are a practical alternative to batteries for storing energy." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of moment of inertia and Newton's second law for rotation. [4]
items.answer: (a) 0.00600 kg m² (b) Both convert the same GPE to KE; the hoop has a larger I, so a bigger fraction of the energy goes into rotation and less into translation, giving a lower speed. (c) Flywheels are excellent for short-term, high-power storage (grid frequency control, buses, F1 KERS), but batteries are better for long-duration storage.
items.markingKey: (a) [1 marks] I = ½MR² = 0.00600 kg m² (A1). (b) [3 marks] Both convert the same GPE to KE; the hoop has a larger I, so a bigger fraction of the energy goes into rotation and less into translation, giving a lower speed. (c) [4 marks] For: high power output and rapid charging; long lifetime with many cycles; no toxic chemicals. Against: energy leaks away by friction (self-discharge); large stresses in fast-spinning rotors – safety containment needed; lower energy per unit mass than batteries. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Flywheels are excellent for short-term, high-power storage (grid frequency control, buses, F1 KERS), but batteries are better for long-duration storage.

items.stem: A uniform 6.0 m plank of weight 300 N rests on two supports, one at each end. A 700 N painter stands 1.5 m from the left end. (a) Draw the forces on the plank. (b) Determine the force from each support. (c) The right support is moved 1.0 m inwards. Calculate how far to the right of this support the painter can walk before the plank tips. (d) Explain why the support forces change as the painter walks.
items.answer: (a) weight 300 N at centre, 700 N at 1.5 m, two upward reactions; (b) moments about left: R_R × 6 = 300 × 3 + 700 × 1.5, R_R = 325 N, R_L = 675 N; (c) tipping about the right support (5.0 m): 700x = 300 × 2.0, x = 0.86 m; (d) the moment of the painter’s weight about each support changes with position.

m / kg | α / rad s⁻²
0.050 | 0.312
0.100 | 0.648

0.200 | 1.285

items.answer: (a) α (y) against torque mgr (x); (b) gradient ≈ 32.6 kg⁻¹ m⁻²; (c) 0.0306 kg m²; (d) 0.0306 kg m² ± 6 × 10⁻⁴ kg m²

items.stem: In a laboratory, a 3.0 kg mass on a cord unwinds from a solid flywheel of mass 8.0 kg and radius 0.1 m (I = ½MR²) that turns freely. The system is released from rest. items.answer: (b) 4.20 m s⁻²; (c) 16.8 N; (d) v = 2.90 m s⁻¹, ω = 29.0 rad s⁻¹; energy: mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² gives the same v.

Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Counterweights extend capacity, but structural strength, stability when unloaded and wind limit the safe load.
